result.summary: Pausanias traces Messenian kingship from the fall of the house of Aphareus to Nestor, then to the Dorian conquest, when Cresphontes won Messenia by a trick with lots. His line, the Æpytidæ, ruled after Æpytus avenged him, and later kings founded cults and a harbour.

scenes.title: From Aphareus's sons to Nestor
scenes.summary: After the sons of Aphareus die, Nestor inherits the kingdom. Pausanias argues the sons of Æsculapius were Messenians and notes the Dorians later expelled Nestor's descendants.
scenes.stakes: The kingdom passes as the male line of Aphareus dies out; the Neleids are later driven out.

scenes.title: Cresphontes wins Messenia by lots
scenes.summary: Cresphontes claims Messenia, Theras objects for the sons of Aristodemus, and Temenus rigs the lots with unbaked clay. The Messenians accept Cresphontes.
scenes.stakes: Control of Messenia, contested between Cresphontes and the sons of Aristodemus.

scenes.title: Murder of Cresphontes, return of Æpytus
scenes.summary: Cresphontes moves the court to Stenyclerus and is killed by wealthy rebels with his sons. Æpytus survives, is restored, and punishes the murderers.
scenes.stakes: Cresphontes's life and his family line; Æpytus's survival.

scenes.title: Later kings and their cults
scenes.summary: Glaucus, Isthmius, Dotadas and Sybotas promote religious cults, and Dotadas builds a harbour at Mothone.

alias_notes.explanation: Dynastic name for the descendants of Æpytus, used instead of Heraclidæ.
Descendants of Heracles, the Dorian kings, including Temenus and Cresphontes.

notable_quotes.reason: The clay lots trick by which Cresphontes won Messenia.

analysis.text: Kingship passes through trickery, violence and restoration, showing how Messenian legitimacy is claimed through lineage and piety.
Pausanias draws on Messenian local tradition to present Messenia as a Dorian-ruled land with older heroic roots, countering Spartan-centred accounts.

legacy.text: The story of Cresphontes, Merope and Æpytus inspired Euripides's lost tragedy Cresphontes and later Voltaire's Mérope (1743).

fun_facts.text: The lot trick with clay dissolving in water is a famous folk-motif of cheating in drawing lots.

language_notes.text: Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, were cousins of Idas and Lynceus; the cattle-raiding quarrel ended with Lynceus and Idas dead. Pausanias calls them 'uncles', loosely.
Homer's Iliad (Book 11) has Nestor tend the wounded Machaon, a healer and son of Æsculapius; Pausanias uses Tricca as evidence for Messenian ties.
'Return of the Heraclidæ' means the descendants of Heracles reclaiming the Peloponnese, conquering with the Dorians; 'two generations afterwards' dates it after the Trojan War.
The lots were tokens dropped into a water-filled jar; the first lot to emerge would win Messenia.
Minyæ were an old Greek people linked with Iolcus, home of the Argonauts; Nestor's Neleid line was of this stock.
Æpytidæ means 'descendants of Æpytus', a dynastic name replacing Heraclidæ.

context_notes.text: Pausanias gives Æsculapius (the healing hero) a Messenian mother, Arsinoe, rejecting the version making Coronis his mother, to claim him for Messenia.
Theras, a Theban descendant of Polynices, guarded his nephews, the sons of Aristodemus, who were Spartan founders. He later led settlers to the island Thera.
Cypselus was king of Arcadia, so the boy Æpytus found refuge with his maternal grandfather.
Mothone was a coastal town in southwest Messenia, so a harbour there aided sea trade.

literary_notes.text: Cresphontes' lot 'came out' only because Temenus cheated, so the apparently fair verdict of chance is a fraud.
The lone surviving boy, raised abroad, prepares the later restoration and revenge.
Glaucus is defined by imitation of his father and by exceeding him in piety.
